documents.unit: AI Stewardship Group (Vice Provost for Academic Services and CIO)
documents.title: APU AI Policy: Responsible and Ethical AI Use
documents.summary: APU's student AI policy defines AI types and permits brainstorming, research, editing and study uses only with explicit instructor permission and disclosure. It requires citation, verification and student ownership, treats violations as integrity breaches, and sends course-level rules to instructors. An FAQ adds examples and a supportive tone.
documents.stance_why: AI uses are allowed 'only with explicit instructor permission and proper disclosure/citation', so AI is barred unless permitted; the FAQ's 'APU supports the transparent and ethical use' softens tone but not the permission gate. Instructors set course rules, but the document itself sets this default, so restrict rather than delegates.

units.why: The opening says the policy exists to govern responsible AI use by students; a framework statement of scope, so P56 (institution-wide framework) rather than a stance type.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this sentence. The source opens 'This policy outlines the responsible and ethical use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools ... for Azusa Pacific University (APU) students', a statement of the policy's purpose and scope, so it is a real framework statement. Kept as P56 (informs) as coder A coded it.
units.anchor: outlines the responsible and ethical use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

units.why: The purpose section lists the principles: integrity, responsible use as a learning aid, 'requires transparent disclosure', and critical evaluation. It is a principles preamble, so P56.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P56, actor, phase and modality. They split on unit_stance: A neutral, B permit. The sentence ('upholds APU's academic integrity, promotes responsible AI use ... as a learning aid, requires transparent disclosure') pairs promotion with integrity and disclosure duties, so as a purpose statement it takes no single position on use: neutral.
units.anchor: upholds APU’s academic integrity, promotes responsible AI use

units.why: The definition sets what counts as AI tools for the policy's scope, so P61.
units.anchor: Software, applications, or platforms that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence

units.why: Defines generative AI ('capable of creating new content') with Gemini as example; a definition fixing scope, P61.
units.anchor: AI tools capable of creating new content (e.g., text, images, code, audio) in response to

units.why: Defines a second category, knowledge management/research AI such as NotebookLM; a definition of scope, P61.
units.anchor: AI tools designed to analyze, organize, summarize, and extract information from existing sources provided by

units.why: The Permitted Uses sentence lists the uses students may make of AI: 'brainstorming, research support, grammar/style editing, study aids, and learning/exploration'. The permission-and-disclosure condition is coded as its own unit, so this unit holds only the list of allowed uses. The list is broad and learning-oriented, so it is coded P12 (AI as a learning aid for understanding); the specific uses are coded separately where the FAQ names them.
units.resolution_why: A coded P15 (brainstorming) and B coded P12; actor, phase, modality and stance agreed. The list mixes brainstorming, research support, editing, study aids and 'learning/exploration', so no single narrow type (P15, P14, P18) covers it. P12 (AI as a learning aid) is the broadest fit, and the FAQ units code brainstorming (P15), study aids (P14) and grammar editing (P18) separately. The normalized policy drops the condition clause, which is a separate unit.
units.anchor: Students may use AI for brainstorming, research support, grammar/style editing, study
units.policy: Students may use AI for brainstorming, research support, grammar/style editing, study aids, and learning/exploration.

units.why: The sentence says uses are allowed 'only with explicit instructor permission and proper disclosure/citation', so without instructor permission AI use is not allowed. That is the fallback rule when the instructor has not granted permission (P06). Student is bound and the modality is must (permission and disclosure are required).
units.resolution_why: A coded P04 with modality may; B coded P06 with modality must. The source does not say who decides (that is the Faculty Discretion unit); it sets the default that AI use needs prior instructor permission, which matches P06 (what applies when nothing has been permitted). 'Only with' makes permission and disclosure conditions that must be met, so must rather than may.
units.anchor: only with explicit instructor permission and proper disclosure/citation
units.policy: Students may use AI only with explicit instructor permission and proper disclosure/citation.

units.why: Prohibited uses include 'submitting AI-generated content as original without permission' and plagiarism; this bans having AI produce submitted work as one's own, P19.
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated content as original without permission
units.policy: Submitting AI-generated content as original without permission is a violation.

units.why: Names 'unauthorized collaboration' and 'misrepresentation' as violations; unauthorized AI use treated as misconduct, P36.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this clause. The Prohibited Uses sentence lists 'misrepresentation, plagiarism, unauthorized collaboration' as violations, which is a rule about what counts as AI misconduct, so it is a real policy statement. Kept as P36 (unauthorized AI use is misconduct) as A coded it.
units.anchor: misrepresentation, plagiarism, unauthorized collaboration
units.policy: Misrepresentation, plagiarism and unauthorized collaboration with AI are violations.

units.why: The same list names 'circumventing learning objectives' as a violation, a ban on undermining learning. P41 explains rather than bans and P19 is about submitted output, so P32 (AI must not replace the student's thinking) fits best.
units.anchor: circumventing learning objectives
units.policy: Circumventing learning objectives is a violation.

units.why: The list also names 'violating data privacy' as a violation; a privacy rule, P50.
units.anchor: violating data privacy
units.policy: Violating data privacy is a violation of the policy.

units.why: 'Students must clearly disclose and properly cite AI tool use' when permitted; a disclosure-with-submission rule, P24.

units.why: Students 'must also be prepared to provide prompts and raw AI output if requested'; this is on-request documentation of prompt and output, closest to P25. P26 requires keeping and submitting logs, which this does not say.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P25, actor and modality. Phase: A during-work, B when-misuse. The sentence ('They must also be prepared to provide prompts and raw AI output if requested') belongs to the Transparency and Citation section on work students submit and is not tied to suspected misuse, so during-work.
units.anchor: prepared to provide prompts and raw AI output if requested

units.why: The example APA-style citation includes the tool, year and prompt text, so it is a tool-and-prompt citation rule, P25.

units.anchor: Instructors set course-specific AI policies

units.why: Same sentence tells students to 'seek clarification when questions arise'; ask-first rule, P10.

units.policy: Students seek clarification from the instructor when questions about the AI policy arise.

units.why: 'Students are responsible for the originality, accuracy, and integrity of all submitted work' makes students own what they submit, P29.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P29 and modality must. Phase: A general, B during-work. 'Students are responsible for the originality, accuracy, and integrity of all submitted work' is a duty that applies to the work students submit, so during-work.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for the originality, accuracy, and integrity of all submitted

units.why: 'ensure the final work reflects your own critical thinking' keeps the student as the thinker, P32.

units.why: The closing statement asks students to use AI 'as faithful stewards' in line with Christian values, a values-based principle for AI use, P56.

units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P10, actor and modality. Phase: A course-start, B during-work. 'When in doubt, always ask your professor' is a way of getting expectations clarified, which matches the matched sentence 'seek clarification when questions arise' (both coders: course-start), so course-start for consistency.

units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded the referral to the Writing, Speaking, and Tutoring Center and academic advisor. The source says 'You can also visit the Writing, Speaking, and Tutoring Center or talk to your academic advisor for additional guidance', a recommendation about where to get help on AI expectations. B folded it into the ask-your-professor unit. Kept as a separate may-unit under P10, which is the closest type (getting guidance when unsure).
units.anchor: visit the Writing, Speaking, and Tutoring Center

units.why: The FAQ answers 'What is Azusa Pacific University's official position?' with 'APU supports the transparent and ethical use of generative AI tools.' This is a statement of institutional principle, not a default rule (the default is the permission gate coded P06), so it is a framework principle: P56, informs, all.
units.resolution_why: A coded P02 (permit or encourage by default); B coded P56. The document's default rule is that AI use needs instructor permission, so the sentence cannot be the default stance. It is the university's stated position/principle, which is P56. Actor, phase, modality and unit_stance (permit) agreed.
units.anchor: APU supports the transparent and ethical use of generative AI tools.
units.frag_end: ethical use of generative AI tools.

units.why: The FAQ states that 'any use of AI to generate content (text, images, etc.) is not considered original work and must be properly cited and attributed'. This is a disclosure and citation duty for students, so P24, must. Citation duties are coded unit_stance require, as in the other disclosure units.
units.resolution_why: Both coded P24, student, must, during-work; they anchored different halves of the same sentence. Unit stance: A require, B permit; disclosure and citation duties were coded require by both coders elsewhere, so require. The normalized policy states both halves as the source does.
units.anchor: must be properly cited and attributed
units.policy: AI-generated content (text, images, etc.) is not considered original work and must be properly cited and attributed.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence (A.I.) Classroom Use Policies: A Syllabus Resource for Instructors
documents.summary: A 2024 Office of Curricular Support resource offering instructors three syllabus statements (no, partial, full AI use) plus three levels of assignment makeover and twenty strategies. It restates that any AI use needs prior instructor permission.
documents.stance_why: 'Instructors can choose one of three use options to include in their syllabus', so the document offers tiers for instructors to pick and sets no single stance; per the codebook, tiers mean delegates.

units.why: States APU's Spring 2023 integrity revision: 'any use of A.I. tools must have prior instructor permission', a ban unless permitted, P06 fits (default when permission not given).
units.anchor: any use of A.I. tools must have prior instructor permission

units.why: Instructors 'can choose one of three use options to include in their syllabus', tiers of AI use, P05.
units.anchor: Instructors can choose one of three use options to include in their syllabus

units.why: The syllabus resource says 'Instructors are welcome to modify these statements to fit their course requirements', so the decision about the final wording and the AI rule sits with each instructor. That fits P04 (let each instructor set the rule). Instructor, before-course, may.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this sentence, as P09. The sentence permits instructors to adapt the template statements; it does not require an AI statement in the syllabus (the document's three options make that point separately), so P04 fits better. Kept.
units.anchor: Instructors are welcome to modify these statements to fit their course requirements

units.why: The statements 'are also being added to Syllabus Templates' on the OCS website, so ready-made syllabus AI language is provided; P09 is closest (AI statement in syllabus), though it is not a requirement.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this sentence ('These statements are also being added to Syllabus Templates available on the Office of Curricular Support (OCS) website'), an office action that makes the AI statements available in templates. Real institutional support for syllabus statements, so kept (P09, admin, informs) as B coded it.
units.anchor: These statements are also being added to Syllabus Templates

units.why: Option 1: 'the use of any artificial intelligence (A.I.)-powered programs, unless specifically assigned, is not allowed'; default ban, P01.
units.anchor: unless specifically assigned, is not allowed
units.frag_end: of any kind is an academic integrity violation.

units.why: Option 1 says using AI to 'outline, write, create, or edit assignments and/or tests' is an integrity violation; classification as misconduct, P36.

units.frag_end: of any kind is an academic integrity violation.

units.why: Option 1 extends the ban to writing assistants like Grammarly, Quillbot, WordTune; a prose-tool rule, P18.

units.why: Option 1 rationale: AI 'may provide inaccurate or biased information, and they do not serve your academic development'; false-output warning, P31.
units.resolution_why: The source has one sentence with two claims: 'A.I.-powered programs may provide inaccurate or biased information, and they do not serve your academic development.' A coded the first (P31), B the second (P41). They are different rules, so both are kept as separate units.
units.anchor: A.I.-powered programs may provide inaccurate or biased information

units.why: Option 1 gives the reason that A.I. programs 'may provide inaccurate or biased information, and they do not serve your academic development', a learning rationale; P41.
units.resolution_why: The source has one sentence with two claims, 'A.I.-powered programs may provide inaccurate or biased information, and they do not serve your academic development.' B coded the second claim (P41) and A the first (P31). Kept as a separate unit. B coded unit_stance prohibit; as a rationale it takes no position itself (the ban is a separate unit), so neutral.

units.why: Option 1 tells students to ask when unsure whether a resource violates the policy, P10.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P10, actor and modality. Phase: A course-start, B during-work. 'If you ... are not sure if a resource you have found will violate this policy, please ask your instructor' is about getting expectations clarified, coded course-start as for the same type in the AI policy.

documents.title: Academic Integrity (graduate catalog policy)
documents.summary: The graduate catalog's academic integrity policy contains a single AI sentence listing unpermitted AI-generated materials as a violation. The rest of the long document does not address AI.
documents.stance_why: The sentence 'may not use artificial intelligence (AI) generated materials for work submitted for credit without permission' bans AI unless permitted, so restrict.

units.why: The catalog's integrity violation list says students 'may not use artificial intelligence (AI) generated materials for work submitted for credit without permission'; banned unless permitted, P06.
units.anchor: may not use artificial intelligence (AI) generated materials for work submitted for credit without permission

notes: Only the university layer was found: no school-level or computing-unit AI policy for APU (Department of Computer Science, Engineering, Math, Physics, and Statistics has no AI page); course syllabi deferred. The syllabus resource (Jan 2024) predates the fall 2025 AI policy and requires prior instructor permission for any AI use, consistent with it; it adds the three-option templates and assignment-makeover strategies. The catalog document is the graduate version only and contributes one AI sentence. Reconciliation conventions: disclosure, citation and documentation duties (P24-P26) keep unit_stance require as both coders coded them; verification duties (P31) are neutral. P32 for 'circumventing learning objectives' and P06 for the prior-permission default are closest fits rather than exact ones. No new types proposed by either coder.
